title: Double crochet in depth
subtitle: UK dc — the dense, even workhorse stitch
excerpt: UK double crochet (US single crochet) is the densest worked stitch in the standard set. This tutorial covers the precise move, tension control, working in rows and in the round, and the UK/US naming conflict that catches readers off-guard.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 1. The double crochet as a fabric stitch and amigurumi base.
heroPrompt: A swatch of double crochet in cream DK cotton showing the dense, even fabric texture, natural linen background, 4 mm crochet hook alongside. The stitch columns are clearly visible.

glossaryTerms.definition: UK double crochet (abbreviated dc) is the densest worked stitch: insert hook, pull up a loop, yarn over, pull through both loops. It equals US single crochet — not US double crochet, which is a taller stitch.
Japanese craft of making small crocheted soft toys. Almost always worked in continuous spirals of UK double crochet, worked tightly to keep the stuffing inside.

content.text: UK
double crochet

is the densest standard stitch. Two loops go onto the hook; one yarn over pulls them off together. No loops left open, no loops shared between stitches. The result is a tight, firm fabric — the stitch behind almost every
amigurumi
figure, every dishcloth, and every dense stitch bag.

attrs.title: UK/US naming — read first
attrs.body: UK "double crochet" (dc) equals US "single crochet" (sc). US "double crochet" (dc) is a taller stitch called "treble" in UK convention. If your pattern is from an American source, UK dc and US dc mean completely different heights. The renderer shows both names; this tutorial uses UK terminology throughout.

content.text: Working a double crochet
With one loop on the hook, insert the hook from front to back through the next stitch, going under both top loops (the V-shape at the top of the stitch).
Yarn over: bring the hook under the working yarn from front to back, catching it in the hook throat.
Pull the loop back through the stitch. Two loops on the hook.
Yarn over again.
Pull through both loops on the hook. One loop remains. The double crochet is complete.

Each completed double crochet should have a clear V-shape at the top. If the V looks twisted, the hook went into the wrong place on step 1 (under one loop only, or between stitches instead of through the stitch body).
Working a swatch in rows
Foundation chain: 15 ch. Turn.
Row 1 (turning chain does NOT count): ch 1 (does not count as a stitch), dc into each chain across (15 dc). Turn.
Row 2: ch 1, dc into each stitch across (15 dc). Turn.
Repeat row 2 for 10 rows total. Fasten off. Count the stitches on the last row — they should be 15. If not, work back to find where the count shifted.

attrs.title: The chain-1 turning chain
attrs.body: The chain-1 at the start of a double crochet row does NOT count as a stitch in standard UK practice. Work the first dc directly into the first stitch at the base of the turning chain. At the end of the return row, work the last dc into the last stitch — not into the chain-1.

content.text: Working in continuous spirals

Amigurumi and other small round shapes use double crochet in a continuous spiral: no join at the end of each round, no turning chain. The work grows upwards in a continuous tube, which is why amigurumi figures have a slight seam-spiral that looks like the stitch columns wind around the shape.
Start with a magic ring. Work 6 dc into the ring. Pull the tail to close the ring. Place a stitch marker in the last stitch of round 1.
Round 2: 2 dc in each stitch around (12 dc). Move the marker to the last stitch.
Continue the pattern, moving the marker at the end of every round so you can count the round boundary.
Common mistakes

attrs.heading: Double crochet problems
attrs.intro: Five problems with double crochet and how to fix each.

items.symptom: The swatch gets narrower with each row
items.cause: Working into the turning chain as if it were a stitch, effectively working two stitches into one position and losing a stitch at the other end.
items.fix: Remember: chain-1 does NOT count as a stitch. Work the first dc into the first actual stitch and the last dc into the last actual stitch, not into the chain-1.

items.symptom: The swatch gets wider with each row
items.cause: Working into the turning chain at the start AND into the space below it at the edge, creating an extra stitch.
items.fix: After the turning chain, find the V-loop of the first stitch directly beneath. Work there, nowhere else.

items.cause: Tension is too tight — squeezing each stitch as it is pulled through.
items.fix: Relax the yarn tension through the yarn hand. The hook should glide through each stitch without forcing.

items.symptom: Gaps between stitches in the first few rows
items.cause: The hook is going between the stitch columns rather than through the stitch body.
items.fix: Aim the hook tip directly into the V at the top of each stitch and push through both legs of the V.

items.symptom: In continuous spiral, the round boundary is lost
items.cause: Forgetting to move the stitch marker at the end of each round.
items.fix: Move the marker immediately after working the last dc of each round, before starting the next.

content.text: What to try next

Once the flat swatch is consistent, try the invisible decrease — two dc worked together in one move — which is the shaping tool for every amigurumi piece. From there, a basic amigurumi ball (six dc in a magic ring, increasing to 24, working even rounds, then decreasing back to six) gives you a complete shape in a single afternoon.
